NATIONAL FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) which is identical with ISO/IEC 2022: 1994 `Information technology -- Character code structure and extension techniques' issued by the International Organization for Standardization (1S0) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) jointly was adopted by the Bureau of India-Standards on the recommendations of the Computer Hardware Sectional Committee and approval of the Electronics and Information Technology Division Council. The text of the ISO/IEC Standard has been approved as suitable for publication as an Indian Standard without deviations. Certain conventions are, however, not identical to those used in Indian Standards. Attention is particularly drawn to the following: a) Wherever the words `International Standard' appear referring to this standard, they should be read as `Indian Standard'. Comma (,) has been used as a decimal marker while in Indian Standards, the current practice is to use a point (.) as the decimal marker.

b)

The technical committee responsible for the preparation of this standard has reviewed the provisions of the following International Standards and has decided that these are acceptable for use in conjunction with this standard;

Section 1- General 1 Scope
This Intemationd Standard specifies the structure of 8-bit codes and 7-bit codes which provide for the coding of character sets. The code elements used in the s~cture are common to both the 8-bit and 7-bit codes. The codes use a variety of techniques for extending the capabilities of elementary 8-bit and 7-bit codes. Greater emphasis is given to 8-bit codes in this edition of the Standard than in previous editions because they are now more widely used. The use of common elements in the 8-bit and 7-bit code structure enables any specific .trastsfomsed into art equivalent 7-bit code, and vice versa, in a simple and direct fashion. ISOflEC 4873 conforms .to tie 8-bit code stmcture specified here. specified here, and ISOflEC conforming 8-bit code to be

646 confoms

to the 7-bit code s~cture
Standard.

Note - me coded chm~ter set spcified in ISOflEC 1W6- 1 has a different sticture

not in accordmce witi this htematinnd

The code struc~re facilities specified here include various means of extending the number of control functions and graphic characters available in a code. They dso include techniques to construct and forrndize the definition of specific codes, and to provide a coded identification of the structure and of the constituent elements of such specific codes. Specific codes may dso be identified by means of object identifiers in accordrmce with 1S0 8824, Abstract Synti One (ASN. 1). The form of such object identifiers is specified in annex A. Notation

Individud character sets and control functions intended for use with these 8-bit and 7-bit codes are assumed to be registered in the 1S0 Intemationd Register of Coded Character Sets to be Used with Escape Sequences, in accordance with 1S0 2375 (see annex B). The register includes details to relate individud character sets and control functions with their coded representations, and dso with the associated coded identifications of such character sets. The principles established in this Intemationd Standard may be utilized to form supplementary code sticture example ISOflEC 6429 has followed such a procedure to formulate some parametrized control functions. The use of uniform code structure techniques focthe 8-bit and 7-bit codes s~ified permitting uniform provision for code strucmre in the design of information here has the advantage ofi facilities. For

processing systems,

-- providing standardized methods of calling into use agreed sets of characters, -- allowing the interchange of data between environments that utilise 8-bit and 7-bit codes respectively, -- reducing the risk of conflict between systems required to inter-operate.
Men two systems with different levels of implementation of code structure facilities are required to communicate another, they may do so using tie code structure facilities that they have in common. with one

The codes specified here are designed to be used for data that is processed sequentially in a forward direction. Use of these codes in strings of data which are processed in some other way, or which are included in data formatted for fixed-length record processing, may have undesirable results or may require additional specird treatment to ensure correct interpretation.

2 Conformance
2.1

Types of conformance

Full conformance to a standard means that dl of its requirements ~e met. Conformance will ordy have a unique meaning if the standard contains no options. If there are options within the standard they must be clearly identified, and any claim of conformance must include a statement that identifies those options that have been adopted. This Internationrd Standard is of a different nature since it specifies a large number of facilities from which different selections may be made to suit individurd applications. These selections are not identified in this Intemationrd "Standard, but must be identified at the time that a claim of conformance is made. Conformance to such an identified selection is bown as limited conformance. The selection of facilities from this Intemationd Standard that are to be used in a particular application will generally be included in a specification document, which states the adopted facilities and gives other details necessary to define fully one or more specific codes. Such a specification is said to be in accordance with this Intemationrd Standard (see 10.1). 2.2

5.1

The bits of the bit combinations of the 8-bit code are identified by b8, b~, b6, b5, bd, b3, b2 and bl, where b8 is tie highest order, or most-significant, bit and b ~ is the lowest-order, or least-significant, bit. The bits of the bit combinations of the 7-bit code are identifid by b7, b6, b5, bq, b3, b2 and bl, where b, is the highest order, or most-significant, bit and b ~ is the lowest-order, or least-significant, bit. The bit combinations may be interpreted to represent integers in binary notation, in the range 0 to 255 for the 8-bit code, and in the range O to 127 for the 7-bit code, by attributing the following weights to the individud bits: Bit Weight In this Intematiortd the range 00 to 15. The notations of the form fly are the same as those used to identify code table positions, where x is the column number and y the row number (see 5.2). 52 Ctie

tables

An 8-bit code table consists of 256 positions arranged in 16 columns and 16 rows. The columns and rows are numbered 00 to 15 (see figure 1). A 7-bit code table consists of 128 positions arranged in 8 columns and 16 rows. The columns are numbered 00 to 07 and the rows 00 to 15 (see figure 1). The code table positions are identifid by notations of the fom fly, where x is the column number and y is the row number. By convention, leading zeroes are included in the column and raw numbers (e,g. OYO1). The positions of the code table are in one-to-one correspondence with the bit combinations table position, of the form tiy, is the same as that of the comesponding bit combination. of the code. me notation of a code

53

Nartses of characters

This Intemationd Standard assigns one name to each character. In addition, it specifies an acronym for each control character and for the characters SPACE and DELETE. By convention, only capiti letters, space and hyphen are used for writing the names of the characters. For acronyms only capiti letters and digits me used. It is intended that the acronyms and this convention be retained in dl translations of the text.

Character DELE~ Acronym: DEL Cod4 representation: 07/15

Name: DELETE

DEL was origirtdly used to erase or obliterate an erroneous or unwantd character in punched tape. DEL may be used for media-fill or time-fill. DEL characters may be inserted into, or removed from, a CC-data-element without affecting its information coutent, but such action may affect the information layout andor the control of quipment. 6.2.2 Character ESCAPE Acronym: ESC Coded representation: 01/11

Name: ESCAPE

ESCAPE is a control character used for code extension purposes. It causes the meaning of a limited number of the bit combinations following it in a CC-data-element to be changed. These bh combinations, togethef witi the precdlng bh combination that represents the ESC character, constitute an escape squence. 6.5 Coded single additional control functions
A coded single additional control function shall be either:

-- a standardized single control function, or -- a registered single control function, or -- a private control function.
Each such function shall be represented by an escape sequence (see clatsse 13). 6.5.1 Standartied sin~e control functions

A standardized single control function shall have a permanently assigned meaning. Such a function shrdl be represented by an escape sequence of type Fs (13.2.1). Each such function shall be registered, together with its coded representation, in the 1S0 Intematiortd Register of Coded CharacterSets (see annex B).

Registered

sin@e control functions

A registered single control function shall have a permanently assigned meaning. Such a function shrdl be represented by an escape sequence of type 3Ft (13.2.2). Each such function shall be registered, together with tis coded representation, in the 1S0 International Register of Coded Character Sets (see annex B).
Note - me notation Ft indicates a bit combination in tie range 04/W to 07/14. me escape sequence consists of tie bit combinations ESC 0Z03 .. Ft (13.2,5),

8.2 Elements and structure of the code
An 8-bit code shrdl include a CO and a GO code element, and may dso include some or M of the code elemenEs Cl, G1, G2, and G3 (7.2). If more than two of GO to G3 are included, it shall include appropriate shift functions (7.3) to enable the graphic characters in those sets to be invoked. An 8-bit code may include one or more single additionrd control functions (6.5), or code-identification functions (7.4).

If more than four sets of graphic characters, or more than two sets of control functions, are required in a specific 8:bit code, designation functions may be included within that code to permit other character sets to be designated as code elements GO to G3, CO, or Cl (14.1). 8.3.3 Shift stitus
The shift status is defined m an atibute of a code element GO to G3 that is in an invoked state, and is identified by the name of the-code table area into which the element is invoked i.e. GL or GR. In an 8+bit code ofly one of GO to G3 cart have a GL shift status, and only one of G1 to G3 can have a GR shift status, at each specifid point within a CC-data-element. Characters from any code element GO to G3 that does not have a shift status cannot be represented within a CC-data-element (except by the method of 8.4) until that code element has been invoked; i.e. at any given point within a CC-data-element not more than two of the code elements GO to G3 can be in an invoked state, one in the GL area and one in the GR area.

The three shift functions LS lR, LS2R, and LS3R, which are specified in 8.3.2 for use in 8-bit codes, may dso be used in a 7-bit code. They shrdl only be used in a 7-bit code when their meaning must be preserved during transformation of CC-data-elements from an 8-bit to a 7-bit code (see 11.1). When used in a 7-bh code LSIR, LS2R, and LS3R shall have the same effects as SO, LS2, and LS3 respectively. 9.3.3 shift Statm

The shift status is defined as an attribute of a code element GO to G3 that is in an invoked state. In a 7-bit code only one of GO to G3 can have a shift status at each specific point within a CC-data-element. Characters from any code element GO to G3 that does not have a shift status cannot be represented within a CC-data-element (except by the method of 9.4) until that code element has been invoked, i.e. at any given point within a CC-data-element not more than one of the code elements GO to G3 can be in an invoked state. .,. At the beginning of information interchange either locking-shift functions shall be used to establish the initial shift status, or the shift status at that point maybe undefined (see 10.1). 9.3,4 Interactions of lockin~shift functions

CC-data-elements conforming to a version of this Intemationd Standard are intended to form dl or part of a composite unit of coded information that is interchanged between a sender and a recipient. me identification of the version of tils Intemationd Standard tiat has been adoptd by the originator, and any other identifications needed to define a fully specified code, shall dso be available to the recipient. me route by which such identification is cotnrnunicatd to the recipient is outside the scope of this Intemationd Standard. . 14.4.1

Dynamidly
hrpose

tiefinable

charac~r

ae@ @RCS)

A Dynamically Redefinable Character Set @RCS) is a set of graphic characters the visual appearance of which is s~ified and transmitted prior to the time of use. Such specification may be made expficifly or by a reference. These characters may be rdphabtic, syllabic, idiographic, special symbols or picture element symbols. Once s~ified, a DRCS is regarded m a as a GO, G1, G2 or member of the repenoire of graphic character sets that can be designati by appropriate escape queries G3 code element. The designation 14.4.2 functions specifid in 14.3 are used with an added indicator, SELE~-DRCS, to designate a DRCS.

Specification

men the SELECT-DRCS indicator is included in a designation function of 14.3, the function sh~ designate an identified DRCS of the indicati type as the indicated code element. Annex B
(informative)

The 1S0 hternational register of coded character sek to be used with esmpe sequenms

B.1

The 1S0

kternational

Register

The 1S0 Intemationd Register contains character sets which have been registered in accordance with procedures specified in 1S0 2375. Its purpose is to identify widely used character sits and associate "with each a unique register entry number to identify it, and a unique escape sequence by means of which it can be desigrtatd conveniently. The publication of this Register promotes compatibility in international information interchange and avoids duplication of effort in devdoping application-oriented character sets. Registration provides an identification for a character set -but implies nothing about its status; it may or may not be part of an international or a natiortd standard, or of au application-oriented standard. However, when such a standard is issued subsequent to the registration of a register number and an escape sequence, it is appropriate for these two forms of identification to be specified in the standard.
Nom - ~s-mgiskr dso contins registrations of otier cting syskrns snd of single conwl functions

B.2

New Registrations

If a recognisd body wishes to register a character set, application should be made as requid in 1S0 2375. Any character set can be a candidate for regis~ation as long as it satisfies the technical ~uirements of ISO~ 2022 and tie. f~rmd requirements of 1S0 2375. Its characteristics will determine the type of escape sequence that can ~ dlocatd to it.

B.3

The Registration

Authority

The -re~tration procedure and the maintenance of the Register is performed by art Intemationrd Registration Authority. has been designated by the Council of the Intemationd Organization for Standardization, 1S0, as the Registration ECMA Authority for 1S0 2375. ECMA carries out these duties as a free service to the international data processing community. It advises applicants on the requirements to be met by applications, circulating the applications in conformance with the procedures. It allocates the register number and the escape sequence and finally registers each character set with its spuific escap sequence. After each registration owners of the Register receive the corresponding additiond shee~ of tie Register.
